extracted.intended_audience: college/university mathematics instructors and graduate students interested in equitable, inclusive teaching practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and enacting undergraduate (and similar-level) mathematics courses that disrupt racial/gender hierarchies and broaden participation through relationship-building, classroom norms, data-informed instruction, and inclusive pedagogical moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove barriers and support confidence building
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor's role is to remove barriers that prevent students from reaching their goals, remove judgment, and support confidence building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include not using timed tests, allowing test corrections, and adopting an overall philosophy to support growth rather than punishment; be intentional about policies that reduce stress and enable learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disaggregated classroom participation data
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and use meaningful, disaggregated data that make inequities in classroom participation visible and actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data should show patterns by social markers (race, gender, disability) so instructors can target strategies; case studies (Anne, Gwen) show data prompted change; gather repeated observations across the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss participation importance and design varied participation activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss with students the importance of participation and create activities to support varied forms of participation (e.g., moving rows and columns in Linear Algebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that allow different ways to contribute so students who don't speak spontaneously still have structured opportunities to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wait for multiple hands before calling on students
rubrics_metrics.description: When soliciting responses, wait for multiple students to raise their hands before calling on someone to avoid always calling the first/most vocal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice reduces dominance by a few students and gives less-vocal students time to prepare; paired with other moves, it broadens who speaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement a 'two voices rule'
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that students wait for two other students to participate before they participate again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps prevent repeated domination by a few students and intentionally spaces contributions among more students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly solicit contributions from students who haven't spoken
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask to hear from students who hadn’t spoken yet rather than relying on spontaneous volunteers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an intentional inclusion move; be careful to do so respectfully and with relationship knowledge so it doesn't feel like tokenism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully select students to share out after group work
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick which students share group work intentionally rather than allowing the same volunteers to dominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selection to elevate underrepresented voices; consider randomization or targeted selection based on who hasn't spoken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use turn-and-talk when few/no students are ready
rubrics_metrics.description: When few students are ready to answer, use short peer-to-peer 'turn-and-talk' opportunities to scaffold participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn-and-talk gives students low-stakes space to formulate thoughts before whole-class sharing, increasing broader participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use random selection / pre-selection to disrupt dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use random methods (e.g., birthday rule) to pre-select which student will share from a group to reduce habitual volunteers dominating discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random selection paired with relationship-building reduces stress of being called on unexpectedly; it's an evidence-based move from case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call on students with intentionality and relational knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Call on specific students deliberately and in ways that minimize stress (e.g., after getting to know them), rather than cold calling without rapport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct short activities to learn about students so calling on them is grounded in relationship and reduces anxiety; use as a tool to include quieter students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign competence (Complex Instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tools of Complex Instruction such as 'assigning competence' to elevate the status of specific students purposefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be effective, instructors need awareness (via data) of who is perceived as low-status so the status-elevating moves target the right students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make small, incremental changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid changing everything at once; implement small, incremental changes to teaching practice that accumulate over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gradual shifts are less disruptive and more sustainable; pair small changes with reflection and data to iterate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly communicate rationale for pedagogical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell students why you are teaching the way you are (e.g., share research on active engagement) and explain the purpose of community standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharing rationale helps students make sense of new practices and opens up channels for meaningful feedback and reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center relationship-building, joy, and community care (radical love)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use education as a tool for liberation by committing to 'radical love'—prioritizing joy, shared hope, community care, and transforming unjust structures through teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on abolitionist teaching and disability justice frameworks; center humanity in interactions and course design rather than purely content coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create psychologically safe environments and reduce stress
rubrics_metrics.description: Build classroom environments that reduce stress (which negatively impacts learning) and protect students from stereotype threat and dehumanization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher immediacy, positive interactions, authenticity, and structural policies (e.g., no punitive timed tests) all contribute to safety and better learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show up authentically
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should show up as whole people—bringing appropriate parts of their identities into the classroom to model openness and build trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity fosters reciprocal openness from students, but instructors from marginalized groups may face additional labor and risk; be mindful of context and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'authenticity' to justify discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity is not an excuse for racist/sexist behavior—'not tolerating intolerance' should be a guiding principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid invoking 'free speech' or 'academic freedom' to permit harmful behavior; such conduct undermines relationship-building and student safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and use students' names
rubrics_metrics.description: Make learning student names a priority using strategies like photo rosters, name cards/tents, having students state their name when contributing, using names frequently, and talking before/after class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using names builds immediacy and belonging, helps include less-vocal students, and should be practiced even in large classes as much as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to pronounce names correctly and avoid nicknames
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice correct pronunciation of names and avoid reducing students to nicknames or ignoring names of less familiar students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated mispronunciation or ignoring names are microaggressions that diminish trust; practice privately if needed and correct respectfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know students as people through casual connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage students in brief non-mathematical conversations before/after class or during circulation to learn goals, interests, and challenges; keep notes as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mentor's heuristic: for each negative interaction, aim for three positive ones; focus on building trust, not reprimanding, to foster engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know students as mathematicians via mathematical biographies
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin courses by having students write a mathematical biography addressing their past experiences, course goals, and expertise they bring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompts can be multi-modal (voice/video); information informs instruction, highlights strengths, and enables multimodal assessment design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share your own mathematical biography and transparently explain pedagogical strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should share their mathematical past, struggles, and pedagogical aims so students understand instructor motivations and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency about new techniques encourages student buy-in and fosters reciprocity when asking for feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuinely attend to student thinking; avoid 'fishing' for answers
rubrics_metrics.description: When asking questions, genuinely care about student responses and use their conceptions as the basis for instruction rather than seeking only a predetermined answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use eye contact, authentic follow-up, and body language that communicates interest; student ideas should inform lesson direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build regular informal and formal check-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: Include brief in-class check-ins (e.g., an ice-cream-flavor mood board) and at least one anonymous mid-semester feedback survey (roughly 1/3 in) with questions like 'What is working?', 'What could be improved?', 'Anything else I should know?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share a summary of feedback and proposed revisions with students and invite response; timing should allow you to enact meaningful changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionally build student-to-student community
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure opportunities for students to build relationships with one another (group work, community-building tasks) so they can collaborate outside class and feel belonging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume students will form these ties on their own; scaffold collaborative activities while being mindful of students' varying access needs and prior trauma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage but never force participation; be mindful of access
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote participation while respecting that students may have social anxieties, trauma, or other reasons to decline participation on any given day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design participation options that are inclusive and provide alternatives so students are invited but not coerced; avoid using individual differences to justify inequitable patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-author community agreements early
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitate students authoring 'community agreements' (not 'threats' or top-down rules) early in the course, ideally after a short collaborative problem and reflective discussion using prompts (What went well? What could be improved? Implications?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process should allow 10–20 minutes minimum for whole-class discussion; instructor can reserve right to suggest or veto items. Sample agreements emphasize listening, respectful critique, and attention to speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid punitive 'community standards' and 'Suspicion Discourses'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not frame classroom rules as threats (e.g., 'NO PHONES', 'NO TALKING', 'COPYING = FAILURE')—these create hostile environments and disproportionately target marginalized students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threat-based language undermines trust and is not effective; treat access and accommodations as legitimate supports rather than cheating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multimodality for low-stakes assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow students to complete reflective or biographical tasks via multiple modalities (written paragraph, voice, video) to increase access and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multimodal options broaden participation and accommodate different communication preferences and access needs.
